objectives: Lay out an annual, quarterly, monthly and continuous GRC calendar
Tell KPIs, KRIs and control effectiveness measures apart, and leading from lagging
Define a metric with an owner, source, target and an honest "not measured"
Write a board report that leads with a verdict and asks for decisions

checks.q: A dashboard shows "0 overdue vendor assessments" in green, but the export from the vendor management tool has failed for two months. How should the next report show this metric?
options: Keep it green, since the tool recorded no overdue assessments in the period.
As "not measured", with the reason and the date data is expected back.
Leave it out of the report until the export is fixed and the data is complete.
Carry forward the last successful value, since vendor status changes slowly.
checks.why: A missing value is a gap, not zero and not green. Showing it as green claims something nobody knows; dropping it or carrying an old value forward hides the gap. "Not measured" with a reason and a date is honest and can be acted on.

checks.q: Which of these is a key risk indicator rather than a key performance indicator?
options: Percentage of staff who completed security awareness training by the annual deadline
Number of policies reviewed and re-approved by their named owners this year
Number of internet-facing servers with critical vulnerabilities older than 30 days
Percentage of steering committee meetings held on schedule with a quorum present
checks.why: The other three measure whether the program is doing its own work. Aging critical vulnerabilities on exposed systems track a condition that changes the likelihood of a specific risk, which is what a KRI does.

checks.q: A CISO's draft board paper opens with twelve pages of dashboard charts and ends with "questions welcome". What change matters most?
options: Open with a verdict against appetite, the top risks and their direction, and the decisions needed.
Add charts for the remaining controls so the board can see the whole program in one place.
Replace the charts with a full table of open findings, each with its owner and due date.
Move the paper to an appendix and present the same charts verbally at the meeting instead.
checks.why: A board report is a decision document. Directors need the position against appetite, the few risks that matter and the decisions in front of them, not more operator-level detail.

checks.q: Last quarter 88% of critical controls were reported as fully implemented; this quarter it is 93%. This quarter the team also stopped counting controls on systems being decommissioned. What should the report do?
options: Report the rise to 93% as the quarter's improvement in control implementation.
Average the two quarters to smooth out the change and report about 90%.
Drop the metric for this quarter, since the two figures cannot be compared.
Note the definition change and restate last quarter's figure on that basis.
checks.why: Part of the rise may be a change in counting, not in controls. Saying so and restating the earlier figure on the new definition keeps the trend comparing like with like.

checks.q: Which activity normally belongs in the monthly rhythm rather than the annual one?
options: Refreshing the organization-wide risk assessment and its ratings
Checking which exceptions and risk acceptances expire next month
Reviewing the risk appetite statement with the board of directors
Reviewing and re-approving the full set of security policies
checks.why: Expiring exceptions need a short loop so none lapse unnoticed. Risk assessment refresh, appetite review and policy re-approval are larger exercises usually run once a year.
